title: UNIT 6: SOME IMPORTANT OXYGEN-CONTAINING ORGANIC COMPOUNDS
notes:
✓ The major classes studied are alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters. The unit also covers fats and oils, which are esters of glycerol and fatty acids.

✓ The unit emphasizes functional groups, structural formulas, IUPAC and common nomenclature, physical properties, chemical reactions, preparation methods, uses and important organic reactions such as substitution, addition, elimination, esterification, hydrolysis and oxidation.

title: 6.1 Introduction
notes:
✓ Organic compounds can be classified according to their structures and functional groups. Oxygen-containing organic compounds include alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters.

✓ Alcohols contain the hydroxyl group (−OH) and have many industrial, pharmaceutical and everyday applications. Methanol is an important industrial chemical, while ethanol is the alcohol found in alcoholic beverages.

✓ Ethers contain an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon groups and are relatively resistant to chemical reactions, making them useful as solvents.

✓ Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group (C=O). Aldehydes generally have pungent odors, while many ketones have pleasant or sweet odors.

✓ Carboxylic acids and esters occur naturally in fruits, flowers, fats and oils. Many carboxylic acids are used as food additives, while esters are responsible for many natural flavors and fragrances.

title: 6.2 Alcohols and Ethers
notes:
✓ Alcohols are derivatives of hydrocarbons in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by hydroxyl groups (−OH).

✓ The functional group of an alcohol is the hydroxyl group (−OH), which is directly attached to a carbon atom of an aliphatic system.

✓ General formula of monohydric alcohols:
CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH

◆ Examples
CH₃OH → Methanol
CH₃CH₂OH → Ethanol
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → Propan-1-ol

✓ Ethers contain an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon-containing groups and have the general structure:
R−O−R′

✓ R and R′ may be identical or different alkyl groups.

title: 6.2.1 Classification of Alcohols
notes:
✓ Alcohols are classified according to the number of hydroxyl groups and according to the number of alkyl groups attached to the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group.

◆ BASED ON NUMBER OF −OH GROUPS

✓ MONOHYDRIC ALCOHOLS → Contain one hydroxyl group.
Example: CH₃CH₂OH, ethanol.

✓ DIHYDRIC ALCOHOLS → Contain two hydroxyl groups and are also called diols or glycols.
Example: HOCH₂CH₂OH, ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol).

✓ TRIHYDRIC ALCOHOLS → Contain three hydroxyl groups.
Example: HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH, propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol).

✓ POLYHYDRIC ALCOHOLS → Contain three or more hydroxyl groups.

◆ BASED ON THE CARBON BEARING −OH

✓ PRIMARY (1°) ALCOHOL → The carbon bearing −OH is attached to only one alkyl group.
General structure: R−CH₂−OH.
Example: CH₃CH₂OH.

✓ SECONDARY (2°) ALCOHOL → The carbon bearing −OH is attached to two alkyl groups.
General structure: R−CH(OH)−R′.
Example: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, propan-2-ol.

✓ TERTIARY (3°) ALCOHOL → The carbon bearing −OH is attached to three alkyl groups.
General structure: R₃C−OH.
Example: (CH₃)₃COH, 2-methyl-2-propanol.

title: 6.2.2 Nomenclature of Alcohols
notes:
✓ In the common naming system, the name of the alkyl group is followed by the word alcohol.

◆ Examples
CH₃OH → Methyl alcohol (methanol)
CH₃CH₂OH → Ethyl alcohol (ethanol)

✓ In the IUPAC system, the final 'e' of the corresponding alkane is replaced by 'ol'.

◆ Examples
Methane → Methanol
Ethane → Ethanol

✓ For alcohols containing three or more carbon atoms, the longest carbon chain containing the hydroxyl group is selected as the parent chain. Numbering begins from the end nearest to the −OH group.

◆ Examples
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → Propan-1-ol
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → Propan-2-ol

✓ For polyhydric alcohols, the number of hydroxyl groups is indicated using di-, tri-, etc.

HOCH₂CH₂OH → Ethane-1,2-diol
HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH → Propane-1,2,3-triol.

title: 6.2.3 Physical Properties of Alcohols
notes:
✓ The hydroxyl group is polar because oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen. Alcohol molecules can therefore form hydrogen bonds with one another.

✓ Hydrogen bonding gives alcohols relatively high melting and boiling points compared with hydrocarbons of similar molecular mass.

✓ Lower alcohols such as methanol and ethanol are miscible with water in all proportions because they can form hydrogen bonds with water.

✓ As the carbon chain becomes longer, the solubility of alcohols in water decreases because the non-polar hydrocarbon portion becomes increasingly important.

✓ Dihydric and trihydric alcohols generally have higher boiling points and greater water solubility than monohydric alcohols of comparable molecular mass because they contain more −OH groups.

✓ Branching lowers the boiling point compared with the corresponding straight-chain isomer.

◆ First six monohydric alcohols
Methanol → CH₃OH → bp 64.7 °C
Ethanol → CH₃CH₂OH → bp 78.3 °C
1-Propanol → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → bp 97.2 °C
1-Butanol → CH₃(CH₂)₂CH₂OH → bp 117.7 °C
1-Pentanol → CH₃(CH₂)₃CH₂OH → bp 138 °C
1-Hexanol → CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₂OH → bp 156.5 °C.

title: 6.2.4 Preparation of Alcohols
notes:
✓ Alcohols can be prepared by several general methods.

◆ 1. ACID-CATALYZED HYDRATION OF ALKENES
✓ Water adds across the double bond of an alkene in the presence of an acid such as H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄.

Alkene + H₂O → Alcohol

Example:
2-methylpropene + H₂O → 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

✓ In the addition, hydrogen from water goes to the carbon of the double bond that already contains more hydrogens.

◆ 2. HYDROLYSIS OF ALKYL HALIDES
✓ Warming an alkyl halide with sodium hydroxide produces an alcohol.

RX + NaOH → ROH + NaX

Example:
CH₃CH₂Cl + NaOH → CH₃CH₂OH + NaCl

◆ 3. HYDROLYSIS OF ESTERS
✓ Heating an ester with potassium hydroxide produces an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.

RCOOR′ + KOH → RCOOK + R′OH

Example:
CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + KOH → CH₃COOK + CH₃CH₂OH

✓ The hydrolysis of alkyl halides and esters involves replacement of another group by −OH and therefore represents substitution reactions.

title: 6.2.4.1 Industrial Preparation of Ethanol
notes:
✓ Ethanol is the second member of the monohydric alcohol homologous series and is present in alcoholic beverages such as Tella, Tej, beer, wine, Katikalla, Ouzo, gin and whisky.

◆ ETHANOL BY FERMENTATION
✓ Fermentation is the slow decomposition of carbohydrates such as sucrose, starch and cellulose in the presence of suitable enzymes.

Sucrose + water → Glucose + Fructose

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2CH₃CH₂OH + 2CO₂

✓ Yeast provides enzymes involved in fermentation.

✓ Fermentation generally produces beverages containing about 12–15% ethanol. Higher ethanol concentrations can be obtained by distillation.

✓ In Ethiopia, molasses, a by-product of sugar production, is commonly used as a raw material. In brewing, germinated barley called malt is used.

◆ ETHANOL BY CATALYTIC HYDRATION OF ETHENE
✓ Ethene is reacted with steam at about 573 K and 60 atm in the presence of phosphoric acid catalyst.

CH₂=CH₂(g) + H₂O(g) → CH₃CH₂OH(g)

Catalyst: H₃PO₄
Temperature: 573 K
Pressure: 60 atm.

title: 6.2.4.2 Preparation of Ethanol by Fermentation
notes:
✓ Sugar is dissolved in distilled water, yeast and a small amount of ammonium phosphate or ammonium sulphate are added, and the mixture is kept in a warm place for several days.

✓ Yeast supplies enzymes that convert sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Calcium hydroxide can be used to observe the carbon dioxide produced.

✓ After fermentation, the mixture is filtered and the liquid can be distilled to obtain an ethanol-containing distillate.

✓ Important observations include the characteristic smell of ethanol and its ability to burn.

title: 6.2.5 Chemical Properties of Alcohols
notes:
✓ Chemical reactions of alcohols may involve cleavage of either the O−H bond or the C−O bond.

◆ Important reactions
✓ Reaction with active metals
✓ Oxidation
✓ Dehydration
✓ Reaction with hydrogen halides
✓ Esterification.

title: 6.2.5.1 Reaction of Alcohols with Active Metals
notes:
✓ Alcohols react with active metals such as Li, Na, K and Mg to form metal alkoxides and liberate hydrogen gas.

2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂

Example:
2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂ONa + H₂

✓ The reaction involves cleavage of the O−H bond of the alcohol.

✓ Hydrogen gas can be identified by bringing a flame close to the gas; hydrogen burns with a characteristic pop.

title: 6.2.5.2 Oxidation of Alcohols
notes:
✓ The oxidation products of alcohols depend on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary and on the oxidizing agent used.

◆ PRIMARY ALCOHOLS
✓ Primary alcohols can first be oxidized to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids.

RCH₂OH → RCHO → RCOOH

✓ Mild oxidation, such as heating a primary alcohol with copper, can produce an aldehyde.

✓ Strong oxidizing agents such as acidified KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇ or CrO₃/H₂SO₄ generally oxidize primary alcohols further to carboxylic acids.

Example:
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO → CH₃COOH
Ethanol → Ethanal → Ethanoic acid

◆ SECONDARY ALCOHOLS
✓ Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones.

R−CH(OH)−R′ → R−CO−R′

Example:
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → CH₃COCH₃
Propan-2-ol → Propanone.

◆ TERTIARY ALCOHOLS
✓ Tertiary alcohols are generally resistant to oxidation under normal conditions.

title: 6.2.5.3 Dehydration of Alcohols
notes:
✓ Alcohols undergo dehydration, meaning removal of a molecule of water, to form alkenes when heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄.

Alcohol → Alkene + H₂O

Example:
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O

✓ Ethanol is dehydrated using concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 170 °C.

✓ Secondary and tertiary alcohols generally undergo dehydration under milder conditions than primary alcohols.

✓ General ease of dehydration:
Tertiary alcohol > Secondary alcohol > Primary alcohol.

title: 6.2.5.4 Reaction of Alcohols with Hydrogen Halides
notes:
✓ Alcohols react with hydrogen halides to form alkyl halides and water.

R−CH₂OH + HX → R−CH₂X + H₂O

✓ X = Cl, Br or I.

Example:
CH₃CH₂OH + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br + H₂O

✓ Ethanol reacts with hydrogen bromide to produce bromoethane.

title: 6.2.5.5 Esterification of Alcohols
notes:
✓ Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters and water.

RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O

✓ The reaction is called esterification.

Example:
CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O

Ethanoic acid + Ethanol ⇌ Ethyl ethanoate + Water.

✓ Esterification is a condensation reaction because water is eliminated during formation of the ester.

title: 6.2.6 Structure and Nomenclature of Ethers
notes:
✓ Ethers are compounds in which an oxygen atom is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.

R−O−R′

✓ If R and R′ are identical, the ether is SYMMETRICAL.
✓ If R and R′ are different, the ether is UNSYMMETRICAL.

◆ COMMON NOMENCLATURE
✓ The names of the two alkyl groups are written alphabetically followed by the word 'ether'.

Examples:
CH₃CH₂−O−CH₂CH₃ → Diethyl ether
CH₃−O−CH₂CH₃ → Ethyl methyl ether

◆ IUPAC NOMENCLATURE
✓ Ethers are named as alkoxy-substituted alkanes. The smaller alkyl group attached through oxygen becomes an alkoxy group.

Examples:
CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃ → 1-Methoxypropane
CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ → 1-Ethoxypentane.

title: 6.2.7 Physical Properties of Ethers
notes:
✓ Ethers are polar compounds because the oxygen atom carries a partial negative charge and the carbon atoms bonded to oxygen carry partial positive charges.

✓ However, ethers cannot form hydrogen bonds with one another in the same way alcohols can because they do not contain an O−H bond.

✓ Therefore, ethers generally have much lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Example:
Ethanol has a boiling point of about 78 °C, whereas dimethyl ether, its constitutional isomer, has a boiling point of about −24 °C.

✓ The oxygen atom of an ether can form hydrogen bonds with water, so ethers are more soluble in water than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass.

✓ Ethers are weakly polar and their boiling points are generally close to those of hydrocarbons of similar molecular mass.

title: 6.2.8 Preparation of Ethers
notes:
✓ Two important methods of ether preparation discussed in the textbook are dehydration of alcohols and Williamson ether synthesis.

◆ 1. DEHYDRATION OF ALCOHOLS
✓ Ethanol produces ethene at 170 °C with H₂SO₄, but at about 140 °C two ethanol molecules can form diethyl ether.

2CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ + H₂O

H₂SO₄, 140 °C

◆ 2. WILLIAMSON ETHER SYNTHESIS
✓ An alkyl halide reacts with an alkoxide ion to produce an ether.

RX + R′O⁻ → R−O−R′ + X⁻

Example:
CH₃CH₂Br + CH₃O⁻ → CH₃CH₂OCH₃ + Br⁻

✓ The Williamson method can be used to prepare symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers.

title: 6.2.9 Reactions and Uses of Ethers
notes:
✓ Ethers resemble hydrocarbons in their resistance to chemical reactions.

✓ They generally do not react with oxidizing agents such as K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄ and are not significantly affected by bases.

✓ Ethers can react with proton donors to form oxonium salts.

Example:
R−O−R + HBr → [R−OH⁺−R]Br⁻

✓ When dialkyl ethers are heated with strong acids such as HI, HBr or H₂SO₄, the ether linkage can be cleaved.

Example:
CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ + 2HBr → 2CH₃CH₂Br + H₂O

✓ Because of their good solvent properties and relative chemical inertness, ethers are useful solvents for many organic reactions. They have also been used in medicine, including as inhalation anesthetics.

title: 6.3 Aldehydes and Ketones
notes:
✓ Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl functional group, C=O.

◆ ALDEHYDE
✓ The carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom.
General structure: R−CHO

✓ For methanal, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two hydrogen atoms:
HCHO.

◆ KETONE
✓ The carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.
General structure: R−CO−R′

✓ Aldehydes and ketones are important oxygen-containing organic compounds and commonly participate in addition, oxidation and reduction reactions.

title: 6.3.1 Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones
notes:
◆ ALDEHYDES
✓ The longest carbon chain containing the −CHO group is selected as the parent chain. The suffix −e of the corresponding alkane is replaced by −al.

Examples:
HCHO → Methanal
CH₃CHO → Ethanal
CH₃CH₂CHO → Propanal

✓ The aldehyde carbon is automatically carbon number 1, so its position does not normally need to be stated.

◆ KETONES
✓ The longest chain containing the carbonyl group is selected. The suffix −e of the corresponding alkane is replaced by −one.

Examples:
CH₃COCH₃ → Propanone
CH₃COCH₂CH₃ → Butan-2-one

✓ For higher ketones, the position of the carbonyl group must be indicated by numbering from the end nearest to the carbonyl group.

Examples:
CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃ → Pentan-2-one
CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ → Pentan-3-one.

title: 6.3.2 Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
notes:
✓ The carbonyl group is polar because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon. Oxygen carries a partial negative charge while the carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge.

✓ Aldehydes and ketones therefore interact through dipole-dipole forces and have higher boiling points than non-polar compounds of comparable molecular mass.

✓ Low-molecular-weight aldehydes and ketones are relatively soluble in water because their carbonyl oxygen can form hydrogen bonds with water.

◆ Examples from the textbook
Methanal → bp −21 °C
Ethanal → bp 20 °C
Propanal → bp 49 °C
Butanal → bp 76 °C
Propanone → bp 56 °C
2-Butanone → bp 80 °C
3-Pentanone → bp 101 °C.

✓ Water solubility generally decreases as the hydrocarbon portion of the molecule becomes larger.

title: 6.3.3 Important Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
notes:
✓ The textbook identifies several important reactions of aldehydes and ketones.

◆ ADDITION
✓ Aldehydes and ketones undergo addition reactions at the polar carbonyl group. Important examples include addition of Grignard reagents and addition of alcohols to form hemiacetals and acetals.

◆ OXIDATION
✓ Aldehydes are readily oxidized to carboxylic acids. Ketones are generally resistant to oxidation under ordinary conditions.

◆ REDUCTION
✓ Aldehydes and ketones can be reduced to alcohols. Catalytic hydrogenation and metal hydride reducing agents are important methods.

✓ These reactions distinguish aldehydes and ketones and connect them to alcohols and carboxylic acids.

title: 6.4 Carboxylic Acids
notes:
✓ Carboxylic acids are organic compounds containing the carboxyl functional group, −COOH.

✓ The carboxyl group consists of a carbonyl group (C=O) and a hydroxyl group (O−H) attached to the same carbon atom.

✓ General structure:
R−COOH

✓ For saturated monocarboxylic acids, R may be H or an alkyl group.

◆ Examples
HCOOH → Methanoic acid
CH₃COOH → Ethanoic acid
CH₃CH₂COOH → Propanoic acid.

✓ When R is an aryl group such as phenyl, the compound is an aromatic carboxylic acid.

title: 6.4.1 Structure and Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids
notes:
◆ MONOCARBOXYLIC ACIDS
✓ Contain one −COOH group.

◆ First members
HCOOH → Methanoic acid (formic acid)
CH₃COOH → Ethanoic acid (acetic acid)
CH₃CH₂COOH → Propanoic acid (propionic acid)
CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH → Butanoic acid (butyric acid)
CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH → Pentanoic acid (valeric acid)
CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH → Hexanoic acid (caproic acid)

✓ IUPAC naming → The terminal 'e' of the corresponding alkane is replaced by 'oic acid'.

Example:
Butane → Butanoic acid.

✓ For branched-chain carboxylic acids, the longest chain containing the carboxyl carbon is selected. The carboxyl carbon is always C-1.

Example:
CH₃−CH(CH₃)−CH₂−COOH → 3-methylbutanoic acid.

◆ DICARBOXYLIC ACIDS
✓ Contain two −COOH groups and are named as alkanedioic acids.

Examples:
HOOC−COOH → Ethanedioic acid (oxalic acid)
HOOC−CH₂−COOH → Propanedioic acid (malonic acid)
HOOC−CH₂CH₂−COOH → Butanedioic acid (succinic acid)
HOOC−(CH₂)₃−COOH → Pentanedioic acid (glutaric acid)
HOOC−(CH₂)₄−COOH → Hexanedioic acid (adipic acid).

◆ TRICARBOXYLIC ACIDS
✓ Contain three carboxyl groups. Citric acid is an important example.

◆ AROMATIC CARBOXYLIC ACIDS
✓ The simplest is benzoic acid. Its IUPAC name is benzenecarboxylic acid.

✓ In common nomenclature, positions on substituted benzoic acids can be designated as ortho (o-), meta (m-) and para (p-).

title: 6.4.2 Physical Properties of Carboxylic Acids
notes:
✓ Lower aliphatic carboxylic acids containing up to about nine carbon atoms are liquids, while higher members are generally colorless waxy solids. Benzoic acid and many of its derivatives are colorless solids.

✓ The lower acids have characteristic odors. Methanoic and ethanoic acids have sharp, irritating odors, while butanoic, pentanoic and hexanoic acids have distinctly unpleasant odors.

✓ Carboxylic acids have relatively high melting and boiling points because molecules can form strong hydrogen bonds. Two carboxylic acid molecules can associate through two hydrogen bonds.

✓ Carboxylic acids of four carbon atoms or fewer are miscible with water in all proportions. Water solubility decreases as molecular mass and hydrocarbon chain length increase.

✓ Their boiling points are generally higher than those of hydrocarbons, aldehydes, ketones and alcohols of comparable size because of strong intermolecular attraction.

title: 6.4.3 Chemical Properties of Carboxylic Acids
notes:
✓ Carboxylic acids are weak acids because they ionize only partially in aqueous solution.

RCOOH + H₂O ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H₃O⁺

◆ 1. REACTION WITH ACTIVE METALS
✓ Carboxylic acids react with active metals such as Na, K, Mg and Ca to form metal carboxylates and hydrogen gas.

Example:
2CH₃COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃COONa + H₂

◆ 2. REACTION WITH BASES
✓ Carboxylic acids react with NaOH or KOH to form carboxylate salts and water.

RCOOH + NaOH → RCOONa + H₂O

◆ 3. REACTION WITH CARBONATES AND BICARBONATES
✓ Carboxylic acids react with carbonates or bicarbonates to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

RCOOH + NaHCO₃ → RCOONa + H₂O + CO₂

✓ The evolution of CO₂ is an important test for a carboxylic acid.

◆ 4. REACTION WITH AMMONIA
✓ Carboxylic acids react with ammonia to form ammonium carboxylates.

◆ 5. ESTERIFICATION
✓ Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to form esters and water.

RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O.

title: 6.4.4 Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
notes:
✓ A major method of preparing saturated monocarboxylic acids is oxidation of the corresponding primary alcohols.

◆ 1. OXIDATION OF PRIMARY ALCOHOLS
✓ Primary alcohols are oxidized using agents such as KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇.

RCH₂OH → RCOOH

Example:
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH
Ethanol → Ethanoic acid.

◆ 2. OXIDATION OF ALKYLBENZENES
✓ Alkyl-substituted aromatic compounds can be oxidized under vigorous conditions using KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇. The alkyl group is converted into a carboxyl group.

Example:
Toluene → Benzoic acid.

✓ The size of the alkyl group does not affect the final aromatic carboxylic acid when suitable oxidation conditions are used.

title: 6.4.4.1 Laboratory and Industrial Preparation of Acetic Acid
notes:
✓ Acetic acid, CH₃COOH, is an important carboxylic acid and food preservative.

◆ LABORATORY PREPARATION
✓ Ethanol can be oxidized to ethanoic acid using oxidizing agents such as potassium permanganate or by passing ethanol vapors over copper oxide.

ETHANOL → ETHANOIC ACID
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH

◆ INDUSTRIAL PREPARATION — QUICK VINEGAR FERMENTATION
✓ Large quantities of acetic acid are obtained by fermentation of ethanol. Wooden vats packed with wood shavings moistened with old vinegar are used. Ethanol solution trickles through the material while air is pumped into the system.

✓ Bacteria present in the old vinegar oxidize/ferment ethanol to acetic acid.

✓ The process can produce an acetic acid solution of about 10%, which can then be fractionated to obtain glacial acetic acid.

title: 6.4.5 Fatty Acids
notes:
✓ Fatty acids are carboxylic acids with long hydrocarbon chains. Most naturally occurring fatty acids contain an even number of carbon atoms and are unbranched.

✓ They are classified as SATURATED or UNSATURATED.

◆ SATURATED FATTY ACIDS
✓ Contain no carbon-carbon double bonds.
Examples:
Lauric acid → C₁₂H₂₃COOH
Myristic acid → C₁₄H₂₉COOH
Palmitic acid → C₁₆H₃₁COOH
Stearic acid → C₁₈H₃₅COOH
Arachidic acid → C₂₀H₃₉COOH.

◆ UNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS
✓ Contain one or more C=C double bonds.
Examples:
Palmitoleic acid → One double bond
Oleic acid → One double bond
Linoleic acid → Two double bonds
Linolenic acid → Three double bonds.

✓ The melting point depends on chain length and degree of unsaturation. Saturated fatty acids generally have higher melting points as molecular mass increases. Increasing the number of double bonds generally lowers the melting point.

◆ For an 18-carbon fatty acid
Stearic acid → 69 °C
Oleic acid → 13 °C
Linoleic acid → −5 °C
Linolenic acid → −11 °C.

title: 6.4.6 Uses of Carboxylic Acids
notes:
✓ Carboxylic acids have many household and industrial applications.

◆ ACETIC ACID
✓ Present in vinegar at about 8–10% concentration.
✓ Used in food products and as a food preservative.
✓ Used as a solvent.
✓ Used as a starting material for acetates and acetic anhydride.
✓ Used to prepare vinyl acetate polymers used in paints and adhesives.

◆ LONG-CHAIN CARBOXYLIC ACIDS
✓ Used in the manufacture of soaps, detergents and shampoos.

✓ Other carboxylic acids occur naturally in fruits, foods and plants and are used in food-related applications.

title: 6.5 Esters
notes:
✓ Esters are important oxygen-containing organic compounds that occur widely in nature. Many esters have pleasant smells and are responsible for the flavor and fragrance of fruits and flowers.

✓ Esters are found in apples, pears, bananas, pineapples, strawberries and many other natural products. Oils, fats and waxes of plant or animal origin are also esters.

✓ An ester is a derivative of a carboxylic acid in which the hydroxyl group of the acid has been replaced by an alkoxy group.

✓ General formula:
RCOOR′

✓ R may be hydrogen, alkyl or aryl, while R′ may be alkyl or aryl.

title: 6.5.1 Sources of Esters
notes:
✓ Esters occur naturally in many fruits, flowers, essential oils, fats, oils and waxes.

✓ Many natural fruit fragrances are produced by esters.

◆ Examples
Apple → Isoamyl isovalerate
Pineapple → Ethyl butyrate
Banana → Isopentyl acetate
Orange → Octyl acetate
Grape → Methyl anthranilate
Pear → Isopentyl acetate.

✓ These compounds contribute to characteristic fruit flavors and fragrances.

title: 6.5.2 Nomenclature of Esters
notes:
✓ The name of an ester has two parts.

✓ The first part comes from the alcohol and is named as an alkyl group ending in −yl.

✓ The second part comes from the carboxylic acid and ends in −ate or −oate.

✓ The alcohol-derived part is written first.

◆ General example
RCOOR′

R′−O portion → Alcohol part.
R−CO portion → Acid part.

Example:
CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ → Ethyl ethanoate.

✓ Using the common name of the acid gives a common ester name, while using the IUPAC acid name gives the IUPAC ester name.

title: 6.5.3 Physical Properties of Esters
notes:
✓ Most simple esters are pleasant-smelling substances and are responsible for many fruit flavors and fragrances.

✓ Low-molecular-mass esters are generally non-toxic liquids and can be used as solvents.

✓ Esters are mildly polar compounds. Their physical properties depend on molecular size and structure.

✓ Many esters have relatively low boiling points compared with carboxylic acids because esters cannot form the same strong intermolecular hydrogen-bonding networks as carboxylic acids.

✓ Their pleasant odors make them especially important in perfumes and flavoring industries.

title: 6.5.4 Chemical Properties of Esters
notes:
✓ Two important chemical reactions of esters discussed in the textbook are hydrolysis and reduction.

◆ 1. HYDROLYSIS
✓ Esters react with water to produce a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under acid-catalyzed conditions.

RCOOR′ + H₂O ⇌ RCOOH + R′OH

Acid catalyst: H₃O⁺.

◆ 2. SAPONIFICATION
✓ Base-catalyzed hydrolysis of an ester is called saponification.

RCOOR′ + NaOH → RCOONa + R′OH

✓ Unlike acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, the base-catalyzed process is effectively not reversible under the reaction conditions.

✓ Saponification is important in biological systems and in the digestion of fats, where enzymes catalyze ester hydrolysis.

◆ 3. REDUCTION
✓ Esters can be reduced to primary alcohols using lithium aluminium hydride, LiAlH₄.

RCOOR′ → RCH₂OH + R′OH

Reducing agents:
1. LiAlH₄
2. H⁺.

title: 6.5.5 Preparation of Esters
notes:
✓ The common method of preparing esters is esterification.

✓ A carboxylic acid is heated with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst, usually concentrated H₂SO₄.

RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O

✓ During the condensation reaction, the −OH group from the carboxylic acid and the −H from the alcohol combine to form water.

Example:
CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O

Ethanoic acid + Methanol ⇌ Methyl ethanoate + Water.

✓ Other examples include preparation of ethyl acetate, ethyl butanoate, methyl benzoate and phenyl ethanoate from suitable carboxylic acids and alcohols.

title: 6.5.6 Uses of Esters
notes:
✓ Esters have many practical applications.

✓ Manufacture of perfumes because many esters have pleasant fragrances.
✓ Flavoring agents in cakes, candies, ice cream and soft drinks.
✓ Solvents for oils and fats.
✓ Solvents used in nail polishes, varnishes, paints, gums and resins.
✓ Pharmaceutical applications, including aspirin-related chemistry.
✓ Manufacture of polyesters such as Dacron.
✓ Plasticizers such as octyl phthalate.
✓ Components of natural flavors and essential oils.

title: 6.6 Fats and Oils
notes:
✓ Fats and oils are esters. They are triesters of glycerol and are collectively called triglycerides or triacylglycerols.

✓ Glycerol contains three hydroxyl groups, so it can form three ester bonds with fatty acids.

✓ A triglyceride is called a FAT when it is solid or semi-solid at room temperature.

✓ A triglyceride is called an OIL when it is liquid at room temperature.

✓ Animal triglycerides are usually solid and are commonly called animal fats. Plant triglycerides are generally liquid and are called vegetable oils.

✓ Vegetable oils are different from mineral oils such as petroleum. Mineral oils consist mainly of long-chain hydrocarbons.

title: 6.6.1 Source of Fats and Oils
notes:
✓ Fats and oils occur widely in living organisms.

◆ COMMON ANIMAL SOURCES
✓ Butter
✓ Lard
✓ Tallow
✓ Dairy products and animal tissues.

◆ COMMON VEGETABLE SOURCES
✓ Peanut oil
✓ Soybean oil
✓ Olive oil
✓ Corn oil
✓ Cottonseed oil.

✓ Animal fats are commonly more saturated and solid at room temperature, whereas vegetable oils generally contain a greater degree of unsaturation and are liquid at room temperature.

title: 6.6.2 Structure of Fats and Oils
notes:
✓ Fats and oils are triglycerides formed from glycerol and three fatty acid molecules.

◆ General structure
CH₂−O−CO−R₁
│
CH−O−CO−R₂
│
CH₂−O−CO−R₃

✓ R₁, R₂ and R₃ may be identical or different hydrocarbon groups.

✓ The variation between different fats and oils mainly comes from the fatty acid portions of the triglycerides.

✓ Fats are mainly esters of glycerol with saturated fatty acids, whereas oils are mainly esters of glycerol with unsaturated fatty acids.

◆ Examples
Glyceryl tristearate (stearin) → An important fat.
Glyceryl trioleate (olein) → An important oil.

title: 6.6.3 Physical Properties of Fats and Oils
notes:
✓ Fats and oils have several common physical properties:
✓ They are greasy to the touch.
✓ They have lubricating properties.
✓ They are not readily volatile.
✓ They can burn without leaving an ash residue.
✓ Pure fats and oils are generally colorless, odorless and neutral.
✓ They are lighter than water.
✓ They are immiscible with water.
✓ They dissolve in organic solvents such as benzene, ether and chloroform.

✓ Fats such as butter, lard and tallow are solids at room temperature.

✓ Vegetable oils such as corn, peanut, cottonseed, olive and soybean oils are generally liquids at room temperature.

✓ A higher degree of unsaturation tends to lower the melting point, making a substance more likely to be liquid at room temperature.

title: 6.6.4 Hardening of Oils
notes:
✓ Oils can be converted into harder fats by adding hydrogen across the carbon-carbon double bonds of unsaturated fatty acid chains.

✓ The process is called HYDROGENATION or HARDENING OF OILS.

✓ It is carried out using hydrogen at high pressure in the presence of a catalyst such as nickel or palladium.

Unsaturated oil + H₂ → More saturated fat

Example:
Glyceryl trioleate + 3H₂ → Glyceryl tristearate

✓ Hydrogenation decreases the degree of unsaturation and increases the melting point.

✓ The process is used in the manufacture of margarine and other hard fats.

title: 6.6.5 Rancidity
notes:
✓ Rancidity is the spoilage of fats and oils that produces an unpleasant odor and disagreeable flavor.

✓ Fats and oils are particularly susceptible to deterioration when stored for long periods, at high temperatures and with free access to air.

◆ Rancidity is mainly associated with
✓ Hydrolysis of ester linkages.
✓ Oxidation across carbon-carbon double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids.

✓ Different fats have different resistance to rancidity. Unsaturated fats and oils can be especially susceptible to oxidation.

◆ To reduce spoilage
✓ Use good-quality raw materials.
✓ Process fats and oils before decomposition begins.
✓ Maintain clean and sanitary conditions.
✓ Store products under favorable conditions.
✓ Limit exposure to air and unfavorable temperatures.
✓ Avoid unnecessary prolonged storage.

notes:
✓ OXYGEN-CONTAINING ORGANIC COMPOUNDS → Alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters.

✓ DIHYDRIC → Two −OH groups.

✓ INDUSTRIAL ETHANOL → Fermentation of carbohydrates and catalytic hydration of ethene.

✓ ETHER → R−O−R′.
✓ SYMMETRICAL ETHER → R and R′ are identical.
✓ UNSYMMETRICAL ETHER → R and R′ are different.
✓ WILLIAMSON SYNTHESIS → RX + R′O⁻ → R−O−R′ + X⁻.
✓ ALDEHYDE → R−CHO; carbonyl group bonded to hydrogen.
✓ KETONE → R−CO−R′; carbonyl group bonded to two carbon groups.
✓ ALDEHYDE SUFFIX → −al.
✓ KETONE SUFFIX → −one.
✓ CARBOXYLIC ACID → Contains −COOH.
✓ MONOCARBOXYLIC ACID → One −COOH group.
✓ DICARBOXYLIC ACID → Two −COOH groups.
✓ TRICARBOXYLIC ACID → Three −COOH groups.
✓ CARBOXYLIC ACID IUPAC → Alkane ending −e becomes −oic acid.
✓ CARBOXYLIC ACID → Weak acid; partially ionizes in water.
✓ CARBOXYLIC ACID + Na → Carboxylate salt + H₂.
✓ CARBOXYLIC ACID + NaOH → Carboxylate salt + H₂O.
✓ CARBOXYLIC ACID + NaHCO₃ → Carboxylate salt + H₂O + CO₂.

✓ ACETIC ACID → CH₃COOH; common name of ethanoic acid.
✓ ACETIC ACID INDUSTRIAL PREPARATION → Quick vinegar fermentation of ethanol.
✓ FATTY ACID → Carboxylic acid with a long hydrocarbon chain.
✓ SATURATED FATTY ACID → Contains no C=C double bonds.
✓ UNSATURATED FATTY ACID → Contains one or more C=C double bonds.
✓ ESTER → RCOOR′.
✓ ESTERIFICATION → Carboxylic acid + Alcohol ⇌ Ester + H₂O.
✓ ESTER NOMENCLATURE → Alcohol-derived alkyl name first + acid-derived −ate name second.
✓ ESTER HYDROLYSIS → Ester + H₂O → Carboxylic acid + Alcohol.
✓ SAPONIFICATION → Base-catalyzed hydrolysis of an ester.
✓ ESTER REDUCTION → Esters can be reduced to primary alcohols using LiAlH₄.
✓ FATS AND OILS → Triesters of glycerol and fatty acids called triglycerides.
✓ FAT → Usually solid or semi-solid at room temperature and generally richer in saturated fatty acid residues.
✓ OIL → Usually liquid at room temperature and generally richer in unsaturated fatty acid residues.
✓ HARDENING OF OILS → Hydrogenation of unsaturated oils to produce harder fats.
✓ HYDROGENATION → Addition of H₂ across C=C bonds using catalysts such as Ni or Pd.
✓ RANCIDITY → Spoilage of fats and oils producing unpleasant odor and flavor, mainly through hydrolysis and oxidation.
✓ KEY IDEA → The functional group determines many of the characteristic properties and reactions of an oxygen-containing organic compound.
